nodes.title: Correctional officer mortality in the United States, 2020–2023: Evidence from the National Occupational Mortality Surveillance program
nodes.blurb: After the publication of our paper on law enforcement officer mortality, JC and I collaborated with Matt Logan (Texas State University) to run it back with a new emphasis on correctional officers, using the same NOMS data.

nodes.title: Robust inference and correlates from genetic associations with personality
nodes.effort_note: I was responsible for the prediction analyses in the Add Health data.
nodes.blurb: This was the largest genome-wide association study (GWAS) of the Big Five personality traits EVER. The first and second authors, Ted and Maggie, were wonderful to work with. Final result: Nature.

nodes.title: Inflammation on the Frontlines: Linking Salivary and Blood Biomarkers to Cardiometabolic Health and Physical Performance Parameters in Firefighters
nodes.venue: Journal of Occupational and Environmental Medicine
nodes.blurb: I orchestrated and carried out the lead authors’ desired analytic approach using data on firefighter health, fitness, and biomarkers. I did the R stuff; they wrote up the study.

nodes.title: Striking or Grappling? Comparing Public and Officers’ Perceptions of Police Use of Force
nodes.blurb: As a BJJ practitioner, I had to be part of this project when I heard it was coming down the pike. We partnered with Austin PD to film video vignettes, which we then used to study perceptions of police use of force in two samples—one law enforcement, one general population. Result: both groups found grappling more appropriate than striking… but for different reasons.

nodes.title: Upstream and downstream racial disparities in prison rule violation processes
nodes.venue: Journal of Research in Crime & Delinquency
nodes.blurb: Back in graduate school (before I knew about R or the tidyverse), I was handed a ridiculously large, and dirty, prison dataset to clean. It took well over a year of working at it by hand to flag string entries for the variables of interest. Years later, my prof reached out with an idea to finally use it. This project is the result.

nodes.title: Clarifying methods and interpretations in law enforcement mortality surveillance: Response to Kamal
nodes.blurb: About a week after publishing the piece on law enforcement officer mortality, we received a comment with several methodological critiques. Most simply reiterated what we ourselves had written in the original article’s limitations section, but one was an important note encouraging us to think about within-occupation comparisons, not just between-occupation ones (i.e., LEOs vs. the general public). This response acknowledged that useful tip and presented the results in that format.

nodes.title: Public opinion and the immediate entry dilemma: A factorial survey experiment on active shooter response
nodes.blurb: This was a follow-on to a project Hunter had already published on law enforcement opinion regarding immediate entry. It pushed those ideas out into the sphere of public opinion, drawing on two samples to probe how the public perceives immediate-entry decisions by police, and where and when they judge them to be correct. I was brought on to help with the analysis, but I managed to slip in some cool plots as well.

nodes.title: Mortality among law enforcement officers in the United States: A population-wide analysis of the National Occupational Mortality Surveillance data, 2020-2023
nodes.blurb: After starting at ALERRT, I got interested in officer health and wellness. But the fundamental question of “what does their mortality profile look like?” eluded a straightforward answer with the research on hand. After finding the NOMS data, I knew I had to work on a project that would give the most definitive answer to that question possible. I assembled a merry band of collaborators, and the rest is history.

nodes.title: To what are we inferring? The widespread misuse of inferential testing in the most cited criminology and criminal justice journals
nodes.blurb: This project was Pete Blair’s brainchild. After several unsuccessful attempts to get it published (something to do with the abnormally high level of snarkiness in the prose), I was offered the chance to come on board and push it over the finish line. A cool Sankey plot, an extensive new discussion section on EFA/CDA, and a newly lowered snark level later, we had a winner.

nodes.title: Active attacks with motor vehicles: A short report and case study of the 2025 New Year’s Day attack in New Orleans, LA
nodes.effort_note: The figure from this project is one of my favs.
nodes.blurb: In the early hours of New Year’s Day, 2025, a man drove a truck at high speed into a crowd of revelers on Bourbon Street in New Orleans, LA. In the following weeks, we put together a brief report covering what we knew about such vehicle-based active attacks, using data from ActiveAttackData.org. One standout characteristic of these attacks was the consistently high number of casualties relative to other types (e.g., knife, handgun, rifle).

nodes.title: Stability of aging- and cognition-related methylation profile scores across two waves in Children and Adolescents
nodes.blurb: A very talented graduate student from my time in the Harden Lab (UT) put together this project examining the stability of DNA methylation over time. I helped with some data curation and visualization, but this was all Abby.

nodes.title: Relationships between physiological stress biomarkers and cardiovascular disease risk factors among career firefighters
nodes.venue: Journal of Occupational and Environmental Medicine
nodes.blurb: I orchestrated and carried out the lead authors’ desired analytic approach using data on firefighter health, fitness, and biomarkers. I did the R stuff; they wrote up the study.

nodes.title: Markers of fitness, stress, and cardiometabolic disease risk among law enforcement officers
nodes.venue: Journal of Occupational and Environmental Medicine
nodes.blurb: I orchestrated and carried out the lead authors’ desired analytic approach using data on police officer health, fitness, and biomarkers. I did the R stuff; they wrote up the study.

nodes.title: Do polygenic indices capture ‘direct’ effects on child externalizing behavior? Within-family analyses in two longitudinal birth cohorts
nodes.effort_note: I did all the things. Paige helped.
nodes.blurb: While at the Harden Lab (UT), I orchestrated a project known to my collaborators as the EXIT (EXternalizing and Intergenerational Transmission) Project. It was slow to get going, but it developed into a very interesting analysis of the direct vs. indirect effects (i.e., the intergenerational part) of externalizing polygenic indices. Two cohorts, two types of genetic effects, and a beautiful 2×2 ggplot2 legend were the result… there was an academic paper too, I guess.

nodes.title: Using Risk of Crime Detection to Study Change in Mechanisms of Decision-Making
nodes.blurb: JC had a super interesting idea about perceived arrest risk vs. actual risk. He wrote the paper using data from the Dunedin Longitudinal Study. I just filled in interesting literature-related tidbits about evolutionary psychology.

nodes.title: Self-control is associated with health-relevant disparities in buccal DNA-methylation measures of biological aging in older adults
nodes.blurb: Yayouk, then a postdoc working with Laurel (a former fellow postdoc from the Harden Lab, UT), put together this great analysis of self-control, DNA methylation, and health outcomes in a German cohort and the Texas Twin Project (TTP). I mostly just helped generate the polygenic indices they needed in the TTP.

nodes.title: History of incarceration and age-related neurodegeneration: Testing models of genetic and environmental risks in a longitudinal panel study of older adults
nodes.blurb: This project started out as an idea for a special issue on evolutionary psychology. After selling a few friends on the idea, it morphed until it was no longer appropriate for the venue. We pushed ahead anyway, and it ended up being a great piece on incarceration, genes, and neurodegeneration later in life.

nodes.title: Guidelines for evaluating the comparability of down-sampled GWAS summary statistics
nodes.blurb: During my time with the Harden Lab (UT), I was also an active member of the Externalizing Consortium. One problem with the original publication was that it used restricted 23andMe data, making data sharing practically impossible-ish. We fixed that by removing the restricted data, but then we needed to benchmark its performance. Thus, this paper.

nodes.title: Associations of DNA-methylation measures of biological aging with social disparities in child and adolescent mental health
nodes.blurb: Laurel, a fellow postdoc at the Harden Lab, worked like mad to get two parallel analyses finished before going on maternity leave: same DNA-methylation measures, same kids, two outcomes. This is the mental-health half, which landed in Clinical Psychological Science. While she was on leave, I was tasked with getting both manuscripts polished up and submitted for publication. With a bit of editing and shiny new data visualizations, they sailed through. Laurel is a badass.

nodes.title: Genetic associations with parental investment from conception to wealth inheritance: 30,000 parents in six cohorts
nodes.blurb: We called this the “genetic handoff” project. It was a HUGE multi-cohort effort headed up by Jasmin Wertz, then a postdoc in the Moffitt and Caspi (Temi and Av) Lab. The basic idea was that genes for educational attainment (à la the EA3 polygenic index) would predict all kinds of parenting behaviors across the entire life course. The contribution from JC, Hexuan (both UC), and me was to analyze the two participating cohorts we had data for.

nodes.title: Life-course persistent antisocial behavior and accelerated biological aging in a longitudinal birth cohort
nodes.venue: The International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
nodes.blurb: This project was developed and executed by Stephanie, a postdoc working with Temi and Av (the Moffitt and Caspi Lab). My involvement was light, mostly critical reviews prior to submission. My dissertation work had been closely related to the topics covered in the paper, so the team was nice enough to ask me along for the ride.

nodes.title: Socially stratified epigenetic profiles are associated with cognitive functioning in children and adolescents
nodes.blurb: Laurel, a fellow postdoc at the Harden Lab, worked like mad to get two parallel analyses finished before going on maternity leave: same DNA-methylation measures, same kids, two outcomes. This is the cognitive-functioning half, which landed in Psychological Science. While she was on leave, I was tasked with getting both manuscripts polished up and submitted for publication. With a bit of editing and shiny new data visualizations, they sailed through. Laurel is a badass.

nodes.title: Incarceration, polygenic risk, and depressive symptoms among males in late adulthood
nodes.blurb: This piece was a CASTLE Lab (UC) classic. Hexuan and I proposed the same idea in a lab meeting (he had thought about it more; I just happened to have the same thought and started blabbing about it): incarceration, polygenic risk, depression. Classic GxE. He analyzed the HRS, I analyzed the WLS. It worked out great.

nodes.title: Adolescent criminal justice involvement, educational attainment, and genetic inheritance: Testing an integrative model using the Add Health data
nodes.blurb: Hexuan (UC) led the CASTLE Lab in another great project, looking at the potential deadening effect of adolescent incarceration on educational attainment using the EA3 polygenic index.

nodes.title: Identifying pathways to polyvictimization: Evidence from a longitudinal cohort study of twins from the United Kingdom
nodes.blurb: Shortly after starting to work with JC (UC), I got the opportunity to lead my first big analytic academic project. We partnered with Temi and Av, using their E-Risk study data to examine the genetic contribution to multiple kinds of cognitive functions and psychopathologies. We wanted to know how adjusting for that genetic contribution changed the association between these mental processes and polyvictimization. Long story short: self-control, even after adjusting for genetic contributions, was the best predictor of future polyvictimization.

nodes.title: The propensity for aggressive behavior and lifetime incarceration risk: A test for gene-environment interaction (G×E) using whole-genome data
nodes.blurb: This project really kicked off the CASTLE Lab at the University of Cincinnati. Ryan Motz (UC) was combing through the HRS codebook and found a reference to past incarceration. Using that, Ryan, JC, and Hexuan put together this study to examine the impact of genetic risk for aggression on lifetime incarceration risk. They brought together a great group of collaborators, and before the project was done they also brought in newly minted lab members, myself included, to help with the final writing and editing.

nodes.title: The genome-wide study of human social behavior and its application in sociology
nodes.blurb: This was my first project to lead, ever. And while it didn’t include an analytic component, it definitely pushed me to develop both my ability and my awareness when it came to academic writing. I really enjoyed working on it, even though I tended to overthink it at times. It was a lot of fun to work on with the group that became the CASTLE Lab (UC).

nodes.title: Every contact leaves a trace: Contact with the criminal justice system, life outcomes, and the intersection with genetics
nodes.blurb: My first academic article, ever. I was not the lead author, but I contributed significantly to the writing and conceptualization of the piece. The part I’ll remember more than anything else is that the hook was mine: I used Locard’s exchange principle to describe how criminal justice contact always leaves some kind of mark on the people who experience it. And genetic risk can exaggerate that mark.
